sub.en: Look at the sentences. Which form works in every tense — can, could, or be able to?

items.q: I ___ read a map, but I lose the car park every time.
items.why: can and could exist only in the present and the past. be able to fills in everywhere else — the future, the perfect, after another verb.

items.q: I ___ swim when I was six.
I’ve never ___ remember names.
items.why: There is no “have could”. The present perfect needs be able to.

items.q: Computers will soon ___ scan our brains.
They won’t ___ understand the thoughts, though.
She ___ speak three languages by the time she was ten.
People with speech problems might ___ communicate this way.
There isn’t ___ in the world who can do it.
items.why: RECYCLED from Lesson 20: any- after a negative.

acts.title: Four things everybody believes about the brain
text: MYTH ONE: we use ten per cent of our brains. Nobody has ever found the study this comes from, because there isn’t one. Scans show activity across the whole brain, including during sleep. If ninety per cent were spare, brain injuries would usually be harmless. They are not.

MYTH TWO: you are either a “left-brain” or a “right-brain” person. The two halves do specialise a little — language sits mostly on the left — but nobody has ever been able to divide people into logical and creative types by scanning them. The test you took online was not measuring anything.

MYTH THREE: your memory works like a video. It does not. Every time you remember something you rebuild it, and you rebuild it slightly differently. This is why two people who were in the same room can’t agree about what happened, and why both of them are certain.

MYTH FOUR: adults can’t learn new skills. Children learn languages faster, which is true and unfair. But adults have been able to learn new instruments, new languages and new jobs at every age that anybody has bothered to measure. The advantage children have is time, and the absence of a job.

tts: No, of course they can’t! But it’s an interesting question, because scientists believe computers will soon be able to scan our brains and put our thoughts into words. They won’t be able to understand the thoughts, though.

write.q: Write about your own abilities: 6 sentences. Two with can or can’t, two with could or couldn’t about your childhood, one with “I’ve never been able to…”, and one prediction with “will be able to”.
write.model: I can read a map and I can cook about four things properly. I can’t sing, and everybody in my family agrees about that. I could swim before I could ride a bicycle, which my mother says is unusual. I couldn’t spell at all until I was about fourteen. I’ve never been able to remember names — I recognise faces immediately and then stand there saying nothing. In two years I hope I’ll be able to have this whole conversation in English without stopping.

speak.q: Answer out loud: What can you do that most people can’t? What could you do as a child that you can’t do now? What have you never been able to do? What will you be able to do in two years?
speak.model: I can read a map without a phone. I could touch my toes as a child and I certainly can’t now. I’ve never been able to remember names. In two years I’ll be able to work in English.
